questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
questions.problem: The volume $V$, in gallons, of water in a pool $t$ minutes after the pool starts filling can be modeled by the function $V(t)=5\sqrt{t}+2.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of the water volume when $t=4$ minutes?
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the water volume when $t=4$ minutes is equal to ${V}^{′}(4).$

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\sqrt{t}+2) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5{t}^{\frac{1}{2}}+2) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{t}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{2\sqrt{t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=4,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(4) & =\frac{5}{2\sqrt{4}} \\  & =\frac{5}{2(2)} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the water volume when $t=4$ minutes is $\frac{5}{4}$ gallons per minute.

questions.problem:
The height $h$ (in feet) of a small rocket $t$ seconds after it is launched can be modeled by the function $h(t)=-16{t}^{2}+128t.$ Find the instantaneous rate at which the rocket's height is changing with respect to time at the moment when its height is equal to $256$ feet.

The instantaneous rate of change of the rocket's height when its height is $256$ feet is
{{field-1}} feet per second.
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that the rocket's height is $256$ feet, the time can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(t) & =256 \\ -16{t}^{2}+128t & =256 \\ -16{t}^{2}+128t-256 & =0 \\ -16({t}^{2}-8t+16) & =0 \\ -16(t-4)^{2} & =0 \\ (t-4)^{2} & =0 \\ t-4 & =0 \\ t & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

The instantaneous rate at which the rocket's height is changing when $t=4$ seconds is equal to ${h}^{′}(4).$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $h(t)$ with respect to $t$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-16{t}^{2}+128t) \\  & =-32t+128,\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $t=4$ gives

$$
{h}^{′}(4)=-32(4)+128=0.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the rocket's height is changing when $t=4$ seconds is $0$ feet per second.

questions.problem:
The concentration $C$ (in millimoles per liter) of a chemical in a reactor $t$ minutes after the reaction begins is modeled by the function $C(t)={t}^{3}+25$ for $0\le t\le 10.$ Find the instantaneous rate at which the concentration is changing with respect to time at the moment when the concentration is $150$ millimoles per liter.

The instantaneous rate of change when the concentration is $150$ millimoles per liter is
{{field-1}} millimoles per liter per minute.
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that the chemical's concentration is $150$ millimoles per liter, the time can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}C(t) & =150 \\ {t}^{3}+25 & =150 \\ {t}^{3} & =125 \\ t & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

The instantaneous rate at which the chemical's concentration is changing when $t=5$ minutes is equal to ${C}^{′}(5).$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $C(t)$ with respect to $t$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+25) \\  & =3{t}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $t=5$ gives

$$
{C}^{′}(5)=3(5)^{2}=75.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the chemical's concentration when its concentration is $150$ millimoles per liter is  $75$ millimoles per liter per minute.

questions.knowledge_point: Further Determining Rates of Change in Geometrical Settings
questions.problem:
The lateral surface area $A$ of a cone is increasing. The radius of the base of the cone is $r,$ and the slant height of the cone is always twice its radius. Find the rate of change of the lateral surface area of the cone with respect to its radius.

The rate of change of the lateral surface area of the cone with respect to its radius $r$ is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the lateral surface area of the cone is given by

$$
A=A(r)=\pi rℓ,
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the base of the cone and $ℓ$ is its slant height.

We are given that $ℓ=2r,$ so we can express the area $A$ as a function of the radius $r$ by substituting $ℓ=2r$ into the formula above. We get

$$
A=\pi r(2r)=2\pi {r}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $A(r)$ with respect to its radius $r$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(2\pi {r}^{2}) \\  & =2\pi (2r) \\  & =4\pi r.\end{aligned}
$$

The volume of a cube-shaped container is increasing. Find the instantaneous rate at which the volume of the container is changing with respect to the side length at the moment when the face diagonal of the cube is equal to $10\sqrt{2}\,\text{cm}.$

The instantaneous rate of change at the moment when the face diagonal is $10\sqrt{2}$ centimeters is equal to
{{field-1}} ${\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{cm}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that the face diagonal of the cube is $10\sqrt{2}\,\text{cm}$, its side length $s$ is $10\,\text{cm}.$ Now, the volume of a cube with side length $s$ is given by 

$$
V=V(s)={s}^{3}.
$$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $V(s)$ with respect to $s$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}({s}^{3}) \\  & =3{s}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $s=10$ gives

$$
{V}^{′}(10)=3(10)^{2}=300.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the volume of the container is increasing when the face diagonal is $10\sqrt{2}\,\text{cm}$ is $300\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{cm}.$
